title: West Town Rain
text:
The rain had been settling in since midnight, and by the time <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was through the Spine crossing it had the run of the place. He walked instead of calling a car because the cold on his wrists was the only sensation right now that wasn't machine noise, and the water found the reopened graze above his hip like it had been sent to check on it.

Wood ran straight north. He'd developed a fondness for straight streets two nights back, in the corridor. Straight meant one thing coming at a time instead of everything at once. The rest of the damage kept its own ledger — right grip at ninety-four percent, ribs charging tax on every breath, compute holding at twelve percent — and he read it the way he read anything, flat, cataloguing, because turning himself into a checklist was easier than being a man walking home in the rain with a sword he'd almost lost for good and a bowl of noodles costing more than they should.

Somewhere around <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity>, a memory that wasn't his surfaced. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e2-727a-be75-32648e8aaa47">Rain</entity> on a different street. A door that didn't open the way he expected. He clocked it the way he clocked a targeting ghost — didn't flinch, didn't slow, filed it under *not mine* and kept walking.

*Wonder if the others minded the rain too*, he thought, and folded that away before it could ask to be looked at.

He found five watchers by the time he was two blocks from <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>.

One high — third-floor window over the print shop, glass a few degrees too cold to be doing nothing, a warmth behind it that wasn't the building's own. One in the laundromat doorway, weight on the wrong foot in the specific way of a man trying to look like he hadn't been standing there an hour, a cigarette gone out in his fingers ten minutes back and not relit, because relighting it would mean looking away. One at the corner, pretending a dead terminal was interesting. One down the block, far enough back to be the anchor. One on a roofline — he got that one from the rain, the way it fell different where something stood in it.

The sixth position he didn't have. Not having it told him what it was. A runner doesn't wait at the trap. A runner waits at the exit. The sixth was already behind him.

Six positions. One of them built to leave.

He worked the drone into the picture a full block off — the distance the guess needed to be right. Maybe two of them, held back until he stepped into the cross-street where the walls closed the gap. Doorway, corner, anchor: a clean three-point close, straight out of a manual somebody had clearly made him read once, in a life he couldn't source. The roofline was the one that could move if it had to. And the warm window was the one keeping score.

Which meant somebody, somewhere, was grading this.

*None of them got a passing mark,* he thought, and put both hands in his coat pockets before the thought could finish being a thought — left on the mouth of the saya, right closed around nothing, because <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> was for when the count came out different than this. He walked into the trap at a normal pace. A man who changes his stride the moment he clocks the surveillance has just told the surveillance everything it needed. Left, right, left — the rhythm of the wet pavement, his breathing matched to it, boots finding the beat of a man who'd decided nothing and noticed less.

The cross-street smelled of wet concrete and the ghost of a food stall packed up hours ago. A turret cat sat on a window ledge up the block, watching the rain with the particular dedication of something that has genuinely nowhere better to be.

He crossed under the print shop's window without looking at it, which was its own kind of look. The warmth behind the glass didn't move. Down the block, the man with the dead cigarette had given up the pretense and turned to face the street, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read that too, flat, and filed it, and kept his hands in his pockets.

He had one more block to <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s door, wet through, ribs arguing the whole way, and he did not look back to see whether the sixth position was following or had simply confirmed that it didn't need to.

The drone dropped at 02:16, sixteen inches short.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew what a stun drone at full discharge looked and sounded like. He'd met three, paid for the lesson twice, and the third time had been someone else's problem. This wasn't that. The discharge hit the wet pavement in a cone that died at his boot heel, the arc chasing the surface water and going out. The sound came a half-note low. The light was maybe forty percent of spec. The drone held at ten feet and cycled for a second pass it never made.

A crew that throttles its own emitters isn't trying to drop you. They were testing how he'd react to a charge that looked real and wasn't — and they'd left maybe two seconds between the drone and the first man moving, which meant the test had a clock on his response. Somewhere close a Ghost sat very still, body parked in a doorway or a car, eyes borrowed from the drone, watching his face and his hands.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. That was one answer. He tilted his head thirty degrees and looked at the drone, which was the more interesting one.

"Evening?" he asked — to the drone, which couldn't answer, and to the crew, which could.

The corner man came first. Young, quick, and angry the way people get angry at twenty-two when they're loyal and a stranger is studying someone they respect. He had an arm. Not chrome, not aftermarket — the real thing, a full replacement from mid-upper-arm down, the kind the catalogs listed at Φ8,000 in a good year. This one ran higher: secondary augments in the forearm, override arrays, a grip that indexed its own pressure. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw the maker's seal at the shoulder joint as the kid closed the last ten feet and swung.

KT. Kinetix TerraForm — the market name for the Warptech Systems division that built precision arms for industrial accidents, and for people who wanted to be more than one. The emergency lockout was a three-finger combination on the outside of the wrist. The certification body required it: a manual override a stranger could reach if the wearer went into medical distress. The lockout drew nothing when it sat idle and drew hard when it held; a KT forearm clamped mid-cycle would start climbing in temperature inside the hour, and the kid didn't know that yet, or didn't care. Once the arm was in range, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had a thirty-second window.

He took the swing on his forearm, stepped inside it, wore the bruise he'd expected, and found the lockout.

The arm stopped. Not dropped — locked, mid-swing, fingers splayed, a chrome hand held out like it was offering him something. KT said several words <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wouldn't write down, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said:

"Kinetix TerraForm — that medical lockout is a liability clause, not a warranty gap. You should get <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> to bill Kinetix for the upgrade. At a minimum. Tell them the restraint architecture's degrading — it won't hold once the carrier gets hot."

He let go. The arm unlocked. KT stepped back with the face of a man who's just been told something humiliating, true, and expensive, in that order.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> came out of the doorway, the approach <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had expected, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> was exactly what the name promised: broad-shouldered, honest the way real size makes a man honest, moving with the economy of someone who'd spent years not starting fights he couldn't finish. The BCI port sat at his left temple — an older Meridian Conduct unit. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew them by the housing, a flat gray oval that stood a little proud of the skull. The early Conduct models had a hardware reset built into the outer casing, because the early Conduct models overloaded and needed a physical hand to stop them.

Hardware that protects itself is a rule baked into the certification. A brain interface you could lock with software was one you could lock with hostile software, and hostile software was a thing the 2218 standards body would not allow. So the Conduct had a mechanical failsafe: hit the housing hard enough and it triggered the reset, dropping the wearer into a five-second blank where the body forgot where it was.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> was bringing his left arm up to guard, so his left side was closed. That put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> on the right — the longer way in, but not by much.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came off the hip for the first time tonight, and some old rule he couldn't name woke up and objected before his hand finished the motion. Draw meant cut. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9b-75e1-9656-810a0ad5cd5d">Cut</entity> meant something didn't get up again. He'd spent eleven years arguing with that rule and it never once lost cleanly — it just got quieter, the way a man gets quiet when he's decided to wait you out.

Not to cut, then. To use the pommel — 340 grams, with a striking reach <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had measured across eleven years of arguments with other people's gear. The pommel found the housing at the angle it needed. <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> blinked twice, stepped left when he'd meant to step right, put a hand out and found the laundromat door instead of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, and sat down with his back against it, working through the reset with his eyes half-focused on a wall that wouldn't hold still.

"<entity repo="character" guid="01a02d38-1757-74fd-8eb3-7e497fc642ab">Five</entity> seconds," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told him. "You're fine."

"Yeah," <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> said, from somewhere inside the blank. "I know."

<entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> went back to the hip, and the motion cost more than the draw had — the old rule taking its toll for being ignored, the way it always did, a small flat weight behind the sternum that had nothing to do with the rib. He didn't look at it straight on. He never did. The rib had something to say about the draw and the return, too, and he let both complaints stand in line and moved.

Three down. The corner man's arm still hung locked-then-unlocked at his side, KT's warranty clause doing more work tonight than the man himself. <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> sat against the laundromat door, present tense but not participating. That left the roofline, the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa78-7aab-bac0-6cae2d09f082">anchor down</entity> the block, and the sixth position — the one built to leave, the one he'd never had a location for, only a certainty.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't look up at the roofline. Looking up was an answer, same as changing his stride would have been. He kept his eyes on the street in front of him, on the rain finding the gaps between the streetlight cones, and did the math the flat way, the checklist way, because the other way — the way that wanted to ask why a five-person test crew was throttling its own drones and grading his reactions like a syllabus — was not a place he had time to stand still in tonight.

*Somebody's keeping a scorecard,* he thought, *and I still don't know whose class this is.*

He put that away with the rest of it and kept walking toward <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s door, twelve percent compute and a ninety-four percent grip and a rib that had opinions, carrying all of it the way he carried everything else that wasn't his to put down yet.

Nines was the one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had marked last, which was Nines's whole job. Industrial wrist brace, pneumatic assist — the freight-yard kind, built for sustained load, the kind that starts having opinions about direction when the pneumatic channel pressurizes wrong. Locked to a single axis. Catch the lock while the pneumatic fights the frame, and the brace's own force does the work for you.

The anchor had held through the drone and both entries, which was professional. Nines waited until <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was busy on the right side, then came across the street at a pace that accounted for the rain — careful — leading with the braced arm — honest.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let him commit to the extension, took the inside line, and used Nines's own weight to fold the braced arm up behind his back. The pneumatic fought the frame. The frame locked. Nines took a close look at the whole surface of the street for about four seconds while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held the brace at the angle that kept the joint arguing with itself.

"Locked out," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and let go. The brace cycled and came free. Nines stayed down a moment, one knee on the wet pavement, looking at his own arm like it had betrayed him in a language he didn't speak yet, and said nothing, which was the professional thing to do.

Four locked, dropped, or walking away confused, and none of them bleeding on his account. Eleven years of the same math and it still came out clean, and some nights that felt like proof of something and some nights it just felt like a number he hadn't broken yet. Tonight he didn't have the spare compute to sort which.

The drone had gone up for altitude. The rooftop position hadn't moved, because the rooftop was the override and knew it wasn't needed. Behind <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, the sixth man — the runner — had the easiest task on the street: wait, then carry the news. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned his back to him on purpose, which was the right signal.

*You've earned the exit. Take it.*

He heard <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-17eb-78c8-831a-5ab1ac1c8cf3">Dex</entity>'s footsteps go east at a run — the way a young man runs when he's been handed the best part of any job, the part where he gets to be the one who says what happened.

Four for four, and nobody upstream had blinked yet. That was the part that itched. A crew this careful, throttling its own gear, grading him like a transcript — a crew doesn't throttle its own drones unless it already knows what it's testing for. They don't leave gaps in the timeline unless they're measuring something. Somebody had built this test to fail gracefully, which meant somebody had already priced in that he'd walk through it, and had watched him do it, and had been counting on it the way you count on a thing that's already happened.

The scorecard wasn't for tonight. It was for whoever read it after.

The rain kept finding the gaps between the streetlight cones. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood exactly where he was, in one of those gaps, and understood that the test had never been about whether he could win. It was about what he'd do when he found out someone upstream had already known he would.

He didn't move toward <entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>. He waited for the next move to come from the one position on the street that still hadn't blinked.

The thermal window on the third floor opened at 02:23.

Mira came down — not through the building's front door but by the fire access on the east side — and she came alone, which meant she'd watched the whole thing and decided it was finished. She was 130 feet out when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> first read her clearly: tall the way he remembered from <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity>, gear that was functional first and functional second, a carry stance that said the piece on her hip was neither a prop nor an afterthought.

She stopped at twenty-five feet. Ordinary talking distance for someone not trying to prove she didn't care about distance.

"Kinetix's lockout is contractor-certified," she said, no preamble, because she'd been watching and what got said was part of what she was grading. "The arm costs Φ11,200 with the augment array."

"I know the price," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I know you know." Her voice had the tightness of someone revising an estimate she hadn't expected to revise — not distress. Different things. "<entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity>'s port is a Meridian Conduct first-series. They put out the mechanical-reset advisory in 2221. He's been meaning to get the housing seated deeper."

"Add the seating charge to the bill."

She looked at him a long moment, the way you look at something behaving a little differently than the model said it would.

Then she drew and fired. One round, twenty-five feet, into the upper chest — because she'd read the corridor reports the way any professional reads someone's recent work, and she knew what was under his coat and what it would cost.

The mesh took it. The impact spread full-contact across his upper chest, the way a shoulder meets a door that isn't going to open: both sides came away informed. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took three breaths, slower than usual. The rib made itself heard.

Mira watched him keep walking. One step, two, the stride unchanged. She dropped the weapon to her thigh, then lowered it to the wet pavement and left it there, muzzle toward the drain.

"That was an audition," she said.

"I worked that out," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> has six rounds. You didn't pull it."

"The audition was for <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> and the body. Six rounds, zero fired. I'll note it for the record."

She almost smiled. It didn't quite finish. "Freelance roster, West Town and adjacent. <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>-territory contracts through your fixer — the Húlijing outfit, I assume. Carrier rates, standard."

"No further crews."

"No further crews," she agreed, and that was the line that meant they were actually negotiating and not just reading terms off a card. She had the authority to give it, and she'd expected him to ask. "The arrangement is provisional. Sixty-day reassessment. Standard for a new roster."

"Your crew's hardware goes on <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity>'s account," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The arm, the port, the brace. List price. You billed them to an audition — they walk home whole, or there's no arrangement."

The tightness in her voice shifted once. Not surprise. Recalculation.

"I can authorize the arm," she said. "The port and the brace I have to clear."

"Clear them. Tonight. I'll be at Chen's at seven-thirty for the confirmation."

"They'd have shot you for free, you know?" Mira asked — and that was the one human line, the one that wasn't the job, the one she'd carried the whole way through and decided she was allowed to say now that the terms were closing.

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Tell <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> their hardware is better than their audit of its own weak points. That's a courtesy, not an invoice."

She reached into the inner pocket of her coat and set the roster marker on the planter rim to her right: a lacquered oval, deep red, a gold five-petal blossom pressed into its face, the size of a thumb and heavier than a thing that size had any business being. The weight of something formal. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked it up.

"Any <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> counter in the city seats you," Mira said, back on solid professional ground now, the human line filed and done. "You pay carrier rates like everyone on the roster. The bowl's better than the politics."

"It usually is."

She picked her piece up off the pavement, cleared it, holstered it, and turned to go. Three steps. Then, over her shoulder, into the rain, without looking back:

"<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">The Narrows</entity> desk bought your file last year, freelancer. You should ask the stationer who else subscribes."

Her footsteps went north, and the bracket came apart: <entity repo="character" guid="019f822d-6c16-7027-b8a9-1fea699defd4">Rook</entity> walking off his reset in a slow circle, KT flexing the arm through its range and cursing the manufacturer under his breath, Nines running the brace through two full cycles to make sure the pneumatic had reset. Professionals writing up their after-action. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood on the wet cross-street with the lacquered marker in one hand and a bruise across his chest that was going to have plenty to say over the next three days, and watched them all go.

The turret cat on the window ledge hadn't moved. It had the patience of something that had been watching long before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> showed up and would go on watching long after he left.

He took stock. A third of the city formally open again, carrier rates, one lacquered marker that weighed more than it should — set against sixty days on a reassessment clock, one mesh bruise, and a name in the Narrows subscription list he'd have to do something about. One thing still open: confirm the hardware authorization, seven-thirty, Chen's counter.

He took the long way home.

At 02:41, between the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> strut and the laundry on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity>, his terminal chirped. The work one.

CONTRACT UPDATE — ASSET SCHEDULE, SUBJECT: KYLE.
CLIENT HAS NOTED THE EXECUTION OF THE LOTUS ROSTER ARRANGEMENT, EFFECTIVE 02:23.
CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE TERMS.
CLIENT HAS APPENDED THE MARKER TO THE SUBJECT'S ASSET SCHEDULE.
VALUATION: ONE BOWL, RECURRING.
ADDENDUM: THE AUDITION CREW'S MEDICAL CLAIM (ARM, PORT, BRACE) HAS BEEN FILED WITH LOTUS ACCOUNTS.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ADVISES THAT "RECURRING" IS THE LOAD-BEARING WORD.
ADDENDUM: CLIENT ALSO NOTES THE RIB. THE RIB HAS BEEN NOTED SINCE DAY ONE. COMPENSATION IN SUBSEQUENT POSITIONS: OBSERVABLE.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read the addenda in the rain, the marker in his coat pocket resting against the old folded plate cover he still carried from the alley — one rectangle of lacquer, one of steel, two proofs that the city paid what it owed once in a while. All he wanted from the next four blocks was simple: get home dry, get the rib horizontal, and file the whole roster arrangement under closed before the client found a way to make it recurring in some other, worse sense.

He typed into the amendment field, which he was doing more often now:

NOTED ABOUT THE RIB. MIND YOUR OWN ARCHITECTURE.

The reply came back in six seconds.

ACKNOWLEDGED.
GRATUITY WITHHELD — ITEMIZED: IMPERTINENCE.

He put the terminal away and walked the last four blocks with the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> humming up through the concrete, the turret cats watching from their ledges, the rain making its arrangements with the city's lights. He thought about the <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">Narrows</entity> desk. About a man with half-glasses and <entity repo="entertainment" guid="019d6513-b76e-734f-9702-c716a9412f2e">clean hands</entity> and a drawer marked CLIENTS, UNSOURCED. About the fact that there was a second subscriber now.

The rib had opinions about the pace. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let it talk.

That was tomorrow's problem.
